title: 400 Gold Coins Found at the Bottom of the Sea!
summary:
Imagine diving 60 feet underwater and seeing gold coins sparkling in the sand! That's what happened in 1995 off the coast of Devon, England. Divers found more than 400 gold coins, plus gold jewelry and a lump of pure gold. But for 30 years, no one knew which ship they came from.

Finally, a clue from a pewter bowl and spoon helped solve the mystery. The ship was the Dom van Keulen, a Dutch trading vessel that sank in 1633. It was carrying African gold from Morocco to the Netherlands. The crew survived and saved most of the cargo, but over 400 coins stayed on the seafloor until 1995.

The coins are now at the British Museum. They are pure West African gold made into Moroccan ducats. The discovery helps us learn about 17th-century trade between Africa and Europe. Isn't it cool that treasure can hide underwater for centuries?
why_it_matters: This story shows that history is all around us, buried under our oceans and waiting to be discovered, teaching us about the past.

keywords.explanation: Diving means swimming deep underwater, often with special gear to breathe.
Sparkling means shining with many small bright flashes of light.
Pewter is a grey metal made from tin and other materials, used long ago for plates and bowls.
A trading vessel is a ship that carries goods to buy and sell between different places.
Ducats are gold coins that were used in Europe many centuries ago.
The seafloor is the bottom of the ocean or sea.

The British Museum (one of the world's largest museums, in London) holds treasures from all over the world.
Morocco (a country in North Africa) was famous for its gold trade with Europe in the 1600s.
Article_Structure: WHO: Divers exploring underwater off Devon, England in 1995
WHAT: A discovery of over 400 gold coins, jewelry, and a gold lump from a 1633 shipwreck
WHERE: At the bottom of the sea off the coast of Devon, England, and now at the British Museum
WHY: The Dutch ship Dom van Keulen sank carrying African gold, and the coins lay hidden until divers found them; historians then used a pewter bowl to identify the ship
